subject: ↪️ Nvidia's board game
body_html:
Plus: Jensen's jolt | Monday, November 23, 2026
 
View in browser
 
 
Axios Closer
By Nathan Bomey · Nov 23, 2026

Monday ✅. Well, we didn't see that coming.

Today's newsletter is 912 words, a 3½-minute read.

📈 The dashboard: The S&P 500 closed up 4.7%.

  • Stocks surged on Jensen Huang's shocking return to Nvidia, with the Nasdaq jumping 6.5% as the AI trade sprung back to life.

🔥 Today's stock spotlight: Nvidia (+31%).
 
 
1 big thing: Board game
 

Photo illustration: Aïda Amer/Axios. Photos: Kevin Carter and Jose Sarmento Matos/Bloomberg via Getty Images
 

Nvidia's surprise 180 to reappoint Jensen Huang shocked investors today, sending the company's shares up over 31%.

Why it matters: Corporate governance and business ethics experts say the move exposes the company to legal liability, rendering the board nearly toothless to keep its CEO accountable moving forward.

⚖️ The big picture: "If he can get away with this, what constraints can the board put on his behavior?" Peter Jaworski, a business ethics professor at Georgetown University, tells me.

  • "The whole thing shows a total lack of backbone on the part of that board," says Charles Elson, a corporate governance expert.
  • "And it's an abrogation of any accepted rules of business, which will ultimately harm the organization and its shareholders — and they will be responsible," Elson says.

🥊 Friction point: The move calls into question the nature of the fiduciary duty that boards have to their shareholders.

  • If their duty is exclusively to boost the stock price, they did the right thing — in the short term, at least — after the company had lost more than $2.5 trillion in market cap in recent weeks.
  • But if the company has a duty to stand on principle and exert leadership in the face of public pressure — including from President Trump, who wanted Huang back on the job — then it failed a critical test.

👀 What we're watching: "You're going to have a lot of plaintiff lawsuits," Elson says. "He will continue to be the center of controversy, he'll have congressional inquiries, this will never end."

🗣️ Newly appointed Nvidia chair Harvey Jones said in a statement that the board "believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers."

Go deeper
 
 
2. Jensen's jolt
 

Illustration: Lazaro Gamio/Axios
 

Nvidia shares skyrocketed on Huang's return, reversing an AI-driven market rout that had sent the Nasdaq into correction territory last week.

💰 Stunning stat: Nvidia alone gained almost $945 billion of market value today — more than the total market caps of all but 15 companies on Earth.

📈 The big picture: The Nasdaq index jumped 6.5% after falling 10% last week.

  • The S&P 500 rose 4.7%, paring some of the losses after last week's 8.6% slide.
  • Neocloud stocks dependent on Nvidia's GPUs, like CoreWeave, Nebius and Iren, soared. Data center operators surged and chipmakers rallied, including Applied Digital, AMD, Micron and TSMC.

👀 Yes, but: As noted above, the AI trade's key man is still under plenty of scrutiny.

What we're watching: His reinstatement "changes nothing" about his planned testimony to the House Intelligence, Foreign Affairs and China committees next week, an Intelligence Committee spokesperson says, reports Axios' Stef Kight, Andrew Solender and Kate Santaliz. (Read it.)
 
 
3. Anthropic sits out the party
 

Photo: Leonardo Munoz/AFP via Getty Images
 

Anthropic's IPO last week failed to turn around slumping AI-tied stocks. Today, the resurrected AI trade failed to juice Anthropic shares, Axios' Pete Gannon writes.

  • Why it matters: Nvidia reaffirmed today that it's the most important stock in the AI trade — and it's not even close.

Zoom in: Anthropic didn't join today's party, slipping 1.4%. Its shares closed today at $87.64, just $4.64 above their IPO price.

Between the lines: Theories abound as to why ANT sat out today's rally, including Huang's support for open-source models that could threaten Anthropic's pricing power.

  • There's one central fact: Unlike many of the AI infrastructure stocks rising today that can profit from the AI spending boom, Anthropic sees its growth hinging on its ability to monetize the models it's spending billions to build.

4. 🤝 CrowdStrike strikes
 

Illustration: Sarah Grillo/Axios. Stock: Getty Images
 

CrowdStrike said it agreed to buy cybersecurity firm Zscaler for around $43.9 billion in stock.

  • Why it matters: Cyber consolidation is accelerating as companies seek to defend against both AI-enabled threats and AI-discovered security holes, Axios' Dan Primack writes.

By the numbers: CrowdStrike shares were up over 95% on the year through Friday's close. They sank 8.9% today following the announcement.

💰 Between the lines: CrowdStrike agreed to pay a hefty 34% premium for Zscaler.

  • 🔒 It's a bet that adding Zscaler's network traffic security to its own device protection will pay off as a bundled security offering capable of competing with Palo Alto Networks and Microsoft, William Blair analyst Jonathan Ho writes, per Barron's.
 
 
5. 🗞️ The readout
 

Photo Illustration: Scott Olson/Getty Images
 

🔮 The White House is reviewing a proposed federal rule authorizing prediction markets to allow trading on sports "event contracts." The CFTC rule is expected to face legal opposition from the states, possibly ending up at the Supreme Court. (Bloomberg)

🧂 Nestle CEO Philipp Navratil said the food giant is trying to lower the amount of sugar, salt and fat from its products but that it's "wrong" to call ultraprocessed foods unhealthy. (WSJ)
 
 
6. 🕔 After hours: Blankfein, from the top rope
 

Photo: Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images
 

"Guess you can come back from the graveyard if you're really, really, really indispensable. The NVDA board will not have that opportunity."
— Former Goldman Sachs CEO Lloyd Blankfein, on X.
